name: Vineyard Sunday
description: God's vineyard and the surprising logic of grace.
biblicalBasis: The parable of the workers in the vineyard where all receive equal pay regardless of when they started: 'Are you envious because I am good?' (Matt 20:1-16). The parable of the wicked tenants who kill the owner's servants and finally his son (Matt 21:33-46). Isaiah's song about the vineyard that God planted, tended, and expected fruit from—but it yielded only wild grapes (Isa 5:1-7).
significance: The vineyard is a recurring image of God's people and His expectation of fruit. The workers' parable overturns human notions of justice: God's grace is not wages earned by merit but generous goodness—'the last shall be first.' The wicked tenants warn against taking God's patience for granted. Isaiah's vineyard song is a judgment on barrenness.
liturgicalContext: Green color. Placed in Trinity season. The vineyard metaphor has made this Sunday a natural day to reflect on the relationship between grace and responsibility, gift and fruit.
history: The vineyard motif is one of the most used in church art history—from catacombs to medieval stained glass. Luther used the workers' parable to emphasize grace alone (sola gratia): God does not reward based on merit.
otConnections: Isaiah 5:1-7—the vineyard song as the core text. Psalm 80:9-16 about the vine God planted from Egypt. Hosea 10:1 about Israel as a fruitful vine. Jeremiah 2:21 about the noble vine that became wild branches. These Old Testament texts form the backdrop for Jesus' use of the vineyard metaphor.

references.reason: The day is about God's vineyard and the demand for fruit. The text about recognizing false prophets by their fruits, and that a good tree bears good fruit, is central to understanding what it means to be a fruitful part of God's vineyard.

The day is about God's grace and the call to do the Father's will. The text that not all who say 'Lord, Lord' will enter, but only those who do the Father's will, emphasizes that faith must show itself in action, which is central to the parable of the vineyard workers.

The day is directly named after the parable of the workers in the vineyard (Matt 20:1-16), which is the main text for this Sunday. The text illustrates God's grace and logic where 'the last become first.'

This passage (Matt 20:17-28) follows immediately after the vineyard parable and expands on the theme of service and leadership in God's kingdom, which is central to understanding the parable. It is often part of the reading for this day.

The conclusion of the chapter (Matt 20:29-34) with the healing of the two blind men serves as a practical illustration of Jesus' service and God's grace, which are the main themes of the preceding passages. This passage is often included in the full reading for the day.
The parable of the two sons (verses 28-32) is an introduction to the vineyard parable and emphasizes the theme of who actually does God's will and bears fruit, in contrast to those who only say yes.

The parable of the wicked tenants (verses 33-46) is central to Vineyard Sunday. The text connects to Isaiah's song about the vineyard and includes the conclusion that God's kingdom will be taken from the unfruitful and given to a people who bear fruit, as well as the reference to 'the stone the builders rejected' (verses 42-44).
